results.content: In the closing weeks before the November 3 US congressional midterm elections, 80 percent of Americans polled said the country needs substantial change or “complete and total upheaval” in how it is run, according to the survey of over 1,100 US adults released on Thursday. Democrats and independents are much more likely than Republicans to want a total overhaul of the country’s direction, the survey found, but even Republican voters are still looking for some change. Fuelled by soaring living costs, everyday economics is driving a majority of the electorate, with 85 percent of respondents saying the economy is one of the most significant issues in weighing their vote in the upcoming election.

results.content: Last week, in the United States, there was some good economic news, and investors appeared to respond accordingly. In the second quarter, growth in real gross domestic product was upwardly revised, while inflation eased slightly in August. These factors likely contributed to investors’ expectations that the Federal Reserve is less likely to tighten monetary policy at its next meeting. The result was an initial rise in equity prices before they reverted. Yet, bond yields continued to rise [...] Despite the favorable news on inflation and a reduced expectation for monetary tightening, the yield on the US Treasury’s 10-year bond continued to rise. results.content: Last week brought encouraging news on U.S. inflation. Core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices and is closely watched by the Federal Reserve, rose 3.0% from a year ago in August. Recent trends were even more encouraging. The three-month annualized rate slowed to 2.0%, reaching the Fed’s target for the first time in more than two years, while the six-month annualized rate declined to 2.7%, its lowest since December of last year.
